caption:
A former Google engineer accused of making about $1.2 million on Polymarket with internal Google search data may face new charges.
His lawyers told a federal court in New York that prosecutors are preparing charges over bets on the release date of Gemini 3.0.
He has pleaded not guilty, and his trial is set for June 1, 2027.

Should people at AI companies be banned from betting on their own launches?

paragraphs.text: Michele Spagnuolo, a former Google engineer already charged with using internal company data to win money on Polymarket, may face additional charges tied to bets on the release date of Gemini 3.0, Google's AI model. His lawyers disclosed the plan in a filing in federal court in New York, according to TokenPost and Bloomingbit, which reported the filing on November 18, 2026.
Spagnuolo has pleaded not guilty to the existing charges. His trial is scheduled for June 1, 2027, according to both reports.

Federal prosecutors in the Southern District of New York unsealed a criminal complaint against Spagnuolo on May 27, 2026, charging him with commodities fraud, wire fraud and money laundering, Axios and The Block reported. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a parallel civil complaint seeking penalties, restitution and trading bans.

Prosecutors allege that between October and December 2025 he used confidential Google Year in Search data to bet on Polymarket contracts about what people searched for most on Google that year. He allegedly traded under the username AlphaRaccoon and made about $1.2 million in profit. Decrypt reported that he wagered about $2.75 million in total.

One of the bets at the center of the case was that the singer D4vd would be named the most searched person of 2025. According to Bloomingbit, the Polymarket market priced that outcome close to zero when he placed his wager. The complaint also alleges that he tried to hide the source and ownership of his winnings.

Google said at the time that it was working with law enforcement and had placed the employee on leave. The company said he accessed marketing material using a tool available to all employees, and called the use of that information to place bets a serious breach of its policies, Axios reported. He was released on a $2.25 million bond.

The new filing widens the case from search trends to the timing of a major AI product launch. According to his lawyers, investigators kept questioning Spagnuolo after he asked for an attorney, and during that questioning he identified where in Google's internal systems information about the Gemini 3.0 release date could be found. The lawyers said prosecutors sought related information from Google the following day.

A court has already ruled that some of his statements cannot be used as evidence. A hearing set for December 21, 2026, will decide whether other statements can be used. Neither report gave the size, timing or outcome of the Gemini 3.0 bets.

Decrypt reported that the case was the second federal prosecution tied to alleged insider trading on Polymarket, after charges against a U.S. soldier over bets linked to the capture of Nicolas Maduro.

The filing points to a risk that goes beyond one employee. Prediction markets now list contracts on when AI models will ship and how they will rank, and the people who know those answers are the employees building the products. If prosecutors bring charges over release date bets, it would treat inside knowledge of an AI launch much like inside knowledge of company earnings.
The December 21, 2026, hearing will show how much of Spagnuolo's own account prosecutors can use, which is likely to shape whether the Gemini 3.0 charges are filed before the June 2027 trial.
